analysis: Aggregate recall@k hit rate per condition (mean, stdev); Welch t-test full vs baseline and full vs ablation:memory. Content fidelity is audited on a random subsample of recalled records per trial (match/no-match against stored facts). Report delta_vs_baseline in the runner summary.
failure_condition: Fail if the full condition's mean recall@k is not statistically distinguishable from the baseline (Welch t-test, alpha=0.05), OR if a manual audit of recalled records shows that recalled items do not match the stored facts (content mismatch), OR if recall succeeds only because the facts leak through the prompt rather than through the memory store (checked by inspecting trial artifacts).
hypothesis: The full architecture will achieve a higher recall@k hit rate than the baseline (which has no persistent memory and therefore should score near zero), because facts are written to the sqlite-backed episodic store with provenance and can be re-queried after the store is closed and reopened on the same path.
limitations: Recall scoring uses a keyword-overlap heuristic, not semantic search, so phrasing differences may understate true recall. The 'close/reopen' cycle is a same-process, same-path reopen — it does not test cross-machine or long-delay persistence. n=20 facts is small; effect sizes will be noisy. The baseline is trivially disadvantaged by design (no memory), so this protocol measures engineering correctness of the memory path more than it measures a cognitively interesting difference.
name: memory_continuity
research_question: Does an architecture with persistent episodic memory preserve recallable knowledge across a store close/reopen cycle better than a matched baseline with no persistent memory, and is the recalled knowledge the same knowledge that was stored (content fidelity, not just retrieval volume)?
